newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 8.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Jan 8.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- EAGLE STAR LOW-COST PENSIONS MAY SPARK PRICE WAR

Eagle Star has announced details of low-cost pensions to be made available through its telephone-based sales division. In addition, the company is offering purchasers of the new scheme a refund of their charges should they decide within two years to switch their scheme to another provider. The move is expected to increase pressure on others in the sector to reduce charges.
-- KAWASAKI JOINS ROLLS-ROYCE ENGINE PROJECT

Rolls-Royce has announced that Kawasaki Heavy Industries is to take a stake in the company's Trent 900 programme to manufacture engines for "super jumbo" aircraft. Initially the Japanese company will hold a 6 percent stake in the initiative, which observers believe has a head start on other groups seeking to supply engines for the new Boeing jets. The Rolls-Royce link-up with Kawasaki builds on links that have existed between the companies since the 1970s.
-- SALES BY CENTRAL BANKS LED TO COLLAPSE IN PRICE OF GOLD

A recent sharp fall in the price of gold has been attributed to heavy selling of the precious metal by European central banks. There had been concern that such sales would be made as certain EU member states struggled to meet Maastricht criteria for participation in the planned single currency. Investors now expect the price to remain flat for the balance of 1997. IMF figures to be announced this year on gold reserves held by individual countries should help identify which EU states have been dipping into reserves.
-- BZW TO SWAP EQUITY RESEARCH WITH U.S. FIRM

U.K. investment banking group BZW is to swap research in the field of equities with U.S. retail broking house Smith Barney. The move, aimed at improving BZW's understanding of the U.S. market, will also compensate for a decision not to acquire an American broking firm. Previously Smith Barney had operated a similar strategy with Smith New Court, which lapsed after the brokerage was taken over by Merrill Lynch, a key rival of Smith Barney.
-- OLIVETTI'S PC ARM SET FOR SALE

Olivetti is expected to announce later this week it is selling its loss-making PC division to a group of European investors, including the Centenary Group. The deal is expected to be worth somewhere in the region of 77 million stg and will help to alleviate concerns among investors about the overall group's level of gearing. Olivetti has pledged to embark on a series of asset sales in order to raise funds to further reduce debt.
-- FORD WARNS OF ACTION TO CUT CAPACITY

Ford, faced with increasing European losses, has warned that it will take tough action to reduce capacity. According to the company's European operations chairman Jac Nasser, Ford is close to deciding precisely what action will be necessary. There has been speculation that Ford might close one of its European manufacturing plants, possibly in Britain. Operations in the U.K. and Germany are generally seen as the most likely targets for any capacity reductions.
-- NEW CAR SALES NUMBERS PASS 2M BUT RECOVERY 'PATCHY'

Figures from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders for U.K. car sales have revealed that during 1996 the number sold broke the 2 million level for the first time since 1990. However, the good news was accompanied by a warning from the industry that the recovery had been patchy and that future profits would be threatened by overproduction internationally. Figures due later in January are expected to reveal that British auto exports for 1996 rose some 20 percent.
-- MINISTERS TOLD TO CUT BACK ON EU RED TAPE

A set of guidelines will be presented to government ministers next week by the minister responsible for deregulation, advising them to become involved in the drafting of EU laws at an early stage. Roger Freeman will advise ministers to "think small" with a view to reducing the level of bureaucracy faced by British business. The EU is expected to produce 15 new directives during 1997.
-- LABOUR PLEDGES INFLATION PRIORITY

Labour in its launch of a New Year offensive against government policy has given a pledge that, should it form the next government, it will give the battle against inflation priority over any economic growth targets. The commitment comes in reply to a new Tory advertising campaign highlighting what it sees as contradictions in a number of areas of Labour economic policy. Previously the Conservatives have scored electoral points in focusing attention on concern about Labour tax plans.
-- U.S. INVESTMENT BANKS BREAK RECORDS

Morgan Stanley and Lehman Brothers have become the latest U.S. investment banks to announce record 1996 profits, setting the scene for similar increases from other banks and brokerages due to report figures in the forthcoming weeks. For the year to the end of November Morgan Stanley saw net income rise to 1.03 billion dollars, while at Lehman Brothers the figure was 416 million dollars for the same period. Some observers doubt that 1997 will see these levels sustained.
